title: Mediator
objectives: Move cross-component rules into one coordinator.
Trace events and silent state updates without a feedback loop.
Distinguish owned child components from borrowed coordinator references.

sections.heading: The problem: one form rule spreads across several controls
paragraphs: A save form has a name field, a consent choice, and a save button. The button should be enabled only when the name is nonempty and consent is accepted. An attempted save while disabled must return false and leave the save count unchanged. Start with one function that computes the rule. If the program is just a small procedural form, that single function is enough. The need for a new structure appears when reusable field and button components must participate without learning the private details of one another.

One tempting design gives the name field a button pointer and has it enable the button whenever text appears. Then the consent control also changes the button. The two controls now need to know the same combined rule. If the name field enables the button without checking consent, typing a name bypasses the requirement. If both controls know each other, changes to the form ripple through all of them. We need one owner of the collaboration rule while keeping the controls responsible for their own simple behavior.

sections.heading: Let components report; let the form decide
paragraphs: A mediator is an object that coordinates the interaction of other objects. Here Form is the mediator. NameField stores text and reports a changed event. SaveButton stores whether it is enabled. Neither component needs to call the other. Form knows the rule that combines a filled name with accepted consent, so its changed function recomputes the button state from current facts.

The small Events interface lets NameField report a change without depending on the concrete Form class. The field receives Events& in its constructor: a required borrowed relationship with no null state. Events has a virtual destructor and a pure virtual changed function. Form implements changed using override, so a misspelled or incompatible replacement is caught during compilation. This interface is justified by reusing the same field with another coordinator. If the form had no reusable components, a direct helper function would be simpler.

sections.heading: Follow one change from input to visible state
paragraphs: Form::name takes a string by value and moves it into NameField::set. The move permits the string storage to be transferred instead of copied when possible; it does not turn the string into a raw pointer. set compares the new text with the old text. Equal text returns immediately because it creates no new fact for the coordinator. Otherwise the field stores the new value and then calls events_.changed. That order matters: the mediator must observe the updated field, not yesterday’s text.

changed reads name_.filled, combines that result with accepted_ using &&, and calls save_.enable. Logical AND is true only when both conditions are true. The local ready value means the name condition alone; the final expression still checks consent. The button update is silent: enable stores a bool but does not report another event. The event direction therefore ends after one coordination step. A mediator is not a promise that loops cannot occur; these particular method contracts are what prevent a feedback loop.

sections.heading: Ownership and callbacks must fit together
paragraphs: Form contains NameField and SaveButton by value, so it owns their lifetimes. Its constructor initializes name_ with *this, a reference to the Form being constructed, treated as its Events base. Passing this reference during construction is safe here because the NameField constructor only stores it and does not call changed. Calling back before all Form members had been initialized would make the coordinator read incomplete state. The code deliberately has no such constructor callback.

The field borrows the mediator it lives inside. This creates a relationship cycle in the object graph, but not an ownership cycle: only Form owns the field; the field does not own Form. Copy and assignment are deleted, which also prevents an implicit move constructor in this design. Without that restriction, a default copy of the field reference would still refer to the original Form, and changes in the copied form could update the wrong button. A more flexible movable form would need to rebind every callback relationship during its move operation.

sections.heading: The coordinator owns policy, not every job
paragraphs: Form::submit checks the current button state and returns false if saving is disabled. The successful path increments saved_, a small local stand-in for completed saves in this demonstration. It does not write a file, send a request, or claim durability. The tests use the count to prove that rejected submissions had no effect. In a real form, the save service belongs behind a separate interface; the mediator can call it, but should not absorb file formats, storage retries, and every other subsystem rule.

Consent changes go through accept, which stores the new bool and calls changed. A repeated accept may recompute the button even if nothing changed; recomputing this pure boolean rule is harmless. The name field avoids equal-text notifications to demonstrate a useful event contract. Neither behavior is inherently more correct. What matters is that listeners know whether setters always notify, notify only on actual change, or never notify. Naming and tests should make the policy visible rather than leave users to infer it from a framework.

sections.heading: Control the growth of the mediator
paragraphs: When forms gain dozens of unrelated behaviors, the mediator can become one huge object that knows too much. Divide coordination by purpose: a validation controller can decide readiness, a storage service can save, and a page controller can choose which view is shown. The goal is a clear home for a specific collaboration, not one central object for an entire application. Do not make every event a string if a small typed interface can keep mistakes visible to the compiler.

The lab adds a temporary hold flag. A held form must disable save even with valid text and consent; lifting the hold must recompute from the other conditions. This change belongs in the mediator because neither the field nor the button knows what a hold means. The extension tests preserve both old rejection cases and the save count. The same reasoning is useful in an editor, setup wizard, or simulation control panel: components announce local changes, and a coordinator decides what those changes mean together.

example.title: A form with one readiness policy
requirements: Enable save only for a nonempty name with accepted consent.
Reject disabled submission without changing the saved count.
Keep field and button types independent of one another.
example.design: Form owns its controls and implements a small Events interface. The field reports changes, the mediator reads all relevant state, and the button updates silently.
example.alternative: A single procedural update_ready function is sufficient for a form with no reusable controls. Letting each control directly alter every peer can look shorter initially but duplicates the combined rule and creates fragile dependencies.
invariants: Button readiness equals filled name AND accepted consent after each public change.
Disabled submit leaves the saved count unchanged.
A field callback always reaches its containing live Form.
Button enable does not emit a new changed event.

failures.mistake: NameField enables save whenever text is nonempty.
failures.consequence: Entering Mina can enable save while consent is false.
failures.reason: One component cannot decide a rule that also depends on another state.

failures.mistake: Use a default copy of a Form whose field borrows its mediator.
failures.consequence: A copied field can send changes to the original Form.
failures.reason: Copying a reference preserves its original target rather than rebinding it.

example.verification: The program checks initial rejection, name-only rejection, enabled save, unchanged input, clearing a name, revoked consent, and preserved saved count. It exercises only local synchronous coordination and a small count; it does not test storage, thread safety, or unlimited-count overflow.
example.maintenance: A new condition changes one readiness policy. Review construction, copy/move behavior, and notification contracts whenever components gain callbacks or the form becomes dynamically owned.

diagram.title: A name change recomputes the button
diagram.explanation: Call arrows show synchronous execution order. The Form callback reads the already updated NameField and changes SaveButton. There is intentionally no call from SaveButton back to Form. This sequence describes messages; Form owning both controls is a separate lifetime fact explained beside the code. Form implements the Events mediator interface; NameField sends the call through that interface. The shown sequence uses the actual concrete participants.

focus.title: Store a fact, then report the event
focus.what: This setter changes only the field text and announces a real change.
focus.where: It runs when Form forwards new input to its NameField.
focus.why: The field does not need to know any peer or consent rule.
focus.invariant: Store the new value before notifying; equal input needs no event.
focus.risk: Notify before storage and the mediator sees stale input.
explain: Define a setter that receives its own string value.
The comment identifies the unchanged-input policy.
Return immediately when old and new text are equal.
Move the input into the field owned string.
Call the borrowed coordinator after the new fact is stored.
Close the setter and mark its boundary.

focus.title: Keep the combined rule in the mediator
focus.what: This callback recomputes the complete save-readiness rule.
focus.where: Form implements the Events operation borrowed by NameField.
focus.why: Only the coordinator knows the relationship between text, consent, and the button.
focus.invariant: A public change must end with save enabled exactly when both conditions hold.
focus.risk: If enabling emits changed again, this simple synchronous path can recurse without end.
explain: Define the implementation of the shared changed event.
The comment states that downstream updates are silent.
Read whether the name field has nonempty text.
Enable save only when text is present and consent is accepted.

trace.reason: The default member values satisfy the readiness rule.
The name is filled, but false consent keeps save disabled.
Both conditions now hold; submit increases the count to one.
The event sees the newly empty field and disables save.

trace.state: Restoring Mina then revoking consent: enabled=false.
trace.reason: Every relevant change recomputes the same combined rule.

summary: A mediator gives a collaboration rule one home.
Components can report events without knowing their peers.
Silent updates are a deliberate way to stop feedback loops.
A borrowed back-reference needs copy/move and construction rules.
Keep the mediator focused on coordination rather than all application work.

exercises.prompt: Change the name requirement to at least two characters. Which operation should change, and what cases should be checked?
exercises.hint: The field already owns the definition of filled.
exercises.answer: Change filled to test value_.size() >= 2, then check empty, one-character, and two-character names with consent true. The mediator can keep combining the field result with consent.

exercises.prompt: For a fresh Form, call accept(true), name("Jo"), name(""), name("Al"), accept(false). List enabled() after each call.
exercises.hint: Evaluate the same two conditions after every step.
exercises.answer: The values are false, true, false, true, false. Consent alone is insufficient; later clearing and restoring text changes readiness without changing consent.

exercises.prompt: A maintainer moves events_.changed() before value_=std::move(value). What happens when an empty field first receives Mina with consent already true?
exercises.hint: The callback reads the old field value.
exercises.answer: It sees empty text and leaves save disabled; the setter then stores Mina without another notification. The form ends in an inconsistent state. Restore store-then-notify order and add this regression case.

exercises.prompt: Choose a mediator or direct function for a command-line prompt with two local values and no reusable controls.
exercises.hint: Do not invent peer objects without a requirement.
exercises.answer: A direct function evaluating the two local values is clearer. Introduce a mediator only when independent components need coordinated rules or event handling that would otherwise spread between them.

exercises.prompt: Add a temporary hold condition that disables save. Must NameField or SaveButton learn what hold means?
exercises.hint: The new condition changes readiness, not text storage or bool storage.
exercises.answer: Neither needs to change. Form stores the hold flag and recomputes ready && accepted_ && !held_. Lifting the hold must not bypass an empty name or missing consent; the lab verifies these cases.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a borrowed field-to-Form reference is acceptable even though the relationship graph contains a cycle.
exercises.answer: Form owns its field by value; the field only borrows Form. There is no shared ownership cycle to keep both alive forever. Construction and destruction rules still must ensure the borrowed reference is used only while Form is valid.

lab.task: Add Form::hold(bool) and a held_ flag. Hold disables submission regardless of name and consent. Lifting hold recomputes readiness and must not bypass any original condition. Preserve the original count and readiness checks.
checks: With Mina and accepted consent, hold(true) disables save and rejects submit.
hold(false) restores readiness and allows one further save.
Lifting hold with an empty name leaves save disabled.
lab.answer: The reference solution changes only the Form coordination rule and its public input. It keeps button updates silent and uses changed after altering the flag. A separate policy function is also reasonable if readiness gains more conditions; it should still have one source of truth.

glossary.definition: An object that owns rules for how other components work together.
A function call made back to code supplied or represented by another object.
A state change that deliberately sends no new change event.
A chain of events that returns to its starting point and may repeat.

problem_title: Coordinate components without tying them together

attachment_alignment.epub_section: Mediator: coordinating form controls, mediator and component roles, the authentication-dialog example, and differences from Facade and Observer.
attachment_alignment.intent: Put the rules for collaboration in one mediator so peer components do not need to know and call each other. The EPUB shows form controls whose mutual dependencies make reuse difficult. Its solution makes a dialog responsible for combined behavior while each control reports its own event through a small interface.
attachment_alignment.mechanism: A component completes its local change and notifies a mediator. The mediator interprets the event in the wider context, then calls the components that must react. This central policy replaces peer-to-peer coordination. It does not mean every class belongs in one giant controller; a mediator should cover one coherent collaboration with clear event rules.

roles.responsibility: Let a component report a change without depending on the concrete policy owner. The chapter has one change notification and needs no event string.
Apply the collaboration rule. Form combines name presence with consent before enabling save.
Do local work, then notify. NameField knows Events but has no SaveButton dependency.
Receive policy decisions from the mediator. Its enable operation changes local state without sending another notification.
Create a valid set of collaborators before events occur. The form owns its controls and supplies itself as their mediator.

source_walkthrough: ClientCode creates Component1 and Component2, then constructs ConcreteMediator with their pointers. Its constructor installs itself into both components. When the client calls DoA, Component1 prints its action and notifies event A. The mediator responds by invoking Component2::DoC.

DoC sends event C back to the mediator, but Notify has no C branch, so the nested notification ends. For DoD, the mediator calls DoB and then DoC. Their B and C notifications also have no matching branches. Output.txt therefore shows A followed by C, and D followed by B then C, without endless recursion.

The sender parameter is present but unused in this implementation; the event string chooses the response. The components begin with nullable mediator pointers and must be wired before their methods run. ClientCode deletes the components and mediator itself. The sample separates collaboration from ownership but relies on correct assembly and teardown.
attachment_alignment.adaptation: The new form uses a required Events reference instead of nullable wiring and string events. NameField reports after storing text; Form reads the current field and consent state. SaveButton updates silently, making the no-feedback rule explicit instead of relying on ignored event letters. Form owns both controls and prohibits copying that would leave callbacks bound to the old form. The example adds readiness and submission tests. It omits a graphical toolkit, asynchronous events, and dynamic subscriptions.
attachment_alignment.recognize: Ask where the rule involving more than one component lives. It belongs in Form::changed, not in NameField or SaveButton. Then follow the notification and the resulting update. An object merely calling several helpers is not sufficient; the mediator must replace collaboration rules that would otherwise couple the participating components.

contrast.distinction: A facade offers clients a simpler entry to a subsystem. A mediator coordinates its participants from within; NameField explicitly notifies the Form through Events.

Observer distributes notifications to registered listeners. Mediator owns a collaboration policy, such as when saving becomes legal. Observer can carry mediator events, but a subscriber list is not required here.

teach.action: Draw A, its C callback, D, its B callback, and its C callback. Mark which event names Notify handles and why the other notifications terminate.
Start with empty name and no consent. Enter Mina, then accept consent. Ask why the name alone cannot enable save.
Clear the name and revoke consent in separate trials. Predict enabled and saved values; inspect the silent button update that avoids an event cycle.

checks.question: Why does the supplied DoC notification not keep calling DoC forever?
checks.answer: Notify reacts only to A and D. The C notification reaches no branch and returns.

checks.question: Should NameField learn whether consent was accepted?
checks.answer: No. That would put the shared readiness rule back into a reusable component. It reports its change; Form combines the relevant state.
